name: Armadillo
baseline: IT++ and Newmat (C++ matrix libraries; no BLAS-vs-Armadillo number on the page)
workload: Timed loops of small and medium dense-matrix expressions (A+B, A+B+C+D, A*B*C*D chains, row copy into a submatrix, trans(p)*inv(diagmat(q))*r), 4x4 to 1000x800 doubles, N chosen so each test runs at least 5 seconds.
claimed_speedup: Approximate speed-ups over IT++/Newmat: add two matrices 4x4 15x/10x, 100x100 3.5x/same speed; add four matrices 100x100 6x/1.5x; multiply four matrices (100x80..40x20) 2.5x/10x and (1000x800..400x200) 2.5x/20x; submatrix row copy 4x4 16x/44x, 100x100 2x/4.5x; multi-operation expression 4x4 77x/23x, 100x100 1086x/5x.
hardware: Intel Core2 Duo CPU (2 GHz, 2 MB cache), Linux kernel 2.6.26
tradeoffs: Header-only template library with delayed evaluation (expression templates); big decompositions and large matrix products still call out to LAPACK/BLAS (OpenBLAS, MKL), so large-matrix speed depends on the linked BLAS rather than on Armadillo itself.
caveats: First-party numbers from a Core2 Duo / Linux 2.6.26 / GCC 4.3.0 setup (an old machine and compiler); compiler flags and exact CPU model are not stated, only a code extract (not the full harness) is shown, and results are shown as graphs with 'approximate speed-up' labels. The baselines are two older, less-used C++ matrix libraries (IT++, Newmat), not BLAS or Eigen, so the guessed BLAS baseline is not what was beaten; the big wins come from avoiding temporaries in small or chained expressions (1086x case is a single-loop fusion), not from faster kernels. Third-party snippets (search result text, arXiv pages not opened) suggest BLAS-linked Eigen can be faster than Armadillo for 512x512 multiplication, so the 'fast' claim is not universal. The repository moved from gitlab.com/conradsnicta/armadillo-code to gitlab.com/armadillo-lib/armadillo-code (redirect).

name: ccache
baseline: uncached compilation (compiler run directly without ccache; the compiler is not named on the page)
workload: Median of 100 individual compilations of ccache.c (-g -O2 -MD plus -I flags) and of c++_includes.cc (nine C++ standard library headers, -MD), comparing no ccache against ccache 3.7.1 in preprocessor, direct and depend mode on first (miss) and second (hit) runs.
claimed_speedup: Cache hit vs no ccache, ccache.c: 0.6988 s uncached vs 0.0048 s direct-mode hit (145.39x) and 0.0247 s preprocessor-mode hit (28.33x). c++_includes.cc: 0.2421 s uncached vs 0.0083 s direct-mode hit (29.10x) and 0.0496 s preprocessor-mode hit (5.09x). Cache misses cost extra: 0.96x on ccache.c, 0.83-0.84x on c++_includes.cc (direct/preprocessor), 0.97x with depend mode.
compiler_and_flags: ccache 3.7.1; compile flags -g -O2 -MD plus -I for ccache.c, -MD only for c++_includes.cc; compiler name and version not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-4690K desktop, standard SSD, Linux
tradeoffs: A cache, so the gain only exists on repeated compilations of unchanged inputs; misses add overhead (page says typically 5%-20%, 1%-3% with depend mode). Needs disk space for the cache and cache-key correctness (non-hermetic builds, timestamps, __TIME__ need care); GPL-3.0-or-later (copyleft) licence.
caveats: First-party numbers measured with ccache 3.7.1 (2019 era; current master is much newer, with BLAKE3 hashing and remote storage) on a Core i5-4690K, with the compiler and its version unstated and no public benchmark script; only two single-file micro-tests, not a whole-project rebuild. The page itself says hit rate and machine memory change the outcome and recommends measuring with and without ccache. The page-level claim in package descriptions is 'often 5 to 10 times speedup'. The comparison is cached versus uncached compilation, not versus another compiler cache such as sccache or distcc, which the page does not measure.

name: ccv (BBF face detector)
baseline: OpenCV default frontal face detector (Haar cascade, default settings; OpenCV version not stated)
workload: Run ccv's bbfdetect and OpenCV's face detector over the CMU frontal face test sets A, B and C (converted to PNG, file list of images) on the same computer, timed with `time`.
claimed_speedup: bbfdetect real 0m9.304s versus OpenCV default face detector real 0m27.977s on the same machine (about 3.0x faster, derived from page data); the SCD doc states OpenCV is about 3 times slower than BBF with a single-thread setup. Accuracy trade: BBF 82.97% detection with 12 false alarms versus OpenCV 86.69% with 15 false alarms.
hardware: Author's own computer, CPU not stated
tradeoffs: BBF detector is lower on detection rate (82.97% vs 86.69% at similar false alarms), and ccv's own FDDB comparison puts OpenCV's frontal detector at 45.18% against BBF at 66.27% at about 250 false positives; C library with a minimal dependency footprint; the source is BSD-3-Clause but the model data and documentation are CC BY 4.0.
caveats: First-party doc written years ago (OpenCV 2.x era) with no CPU model, compiler or flags, and no benchmark script beyond the shown shell commands, so the tier stops at C. The timed run includes image decoding and output for both programs, the OpenCV program and version are not named, and OpenCV's detector was run with default settings, which are not necessarily equivalent to bbfdetect's scale and neighbour parameters. Also ccv's own HOG comparison (dpm.rst) shows OpenCV's HOG pedestrian detector 4.34 times faster than ccv's DPM, and the ccv convnet doc says it chooses correctness over speed. Claim is only about the BBF face detector, not the whole library.

name: Coost co/log
workload: Time or write speed for continuously printing 1 million log lines, single thread against glog on four platforms, and 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads against spdlog on Linux and Windows.
claimed_speedup: vs glog (1 thread, 1 million logs, write speed): win2012 HDD 1.6MB/s vs 180MB/s (112.5x), win10 SSD 3.7MB/s vs 560MB/s (151.3x), mac SSD 17MB/s vs 450MB/s (26.4x), linux SSD 54MB/s vs 1023MB/s (18.9x). vs spdlog (seconds for 1 million logs): linux 1 thread 0.087235 vs 2.076172 (23.8x), 8 threads 0.302088 vs 3.963644 (13.1x); windows 1 thread 0.117704 vs 0.461156 (3.9x), 8 threads 0.406025 vs 1.417387 (3.5x).
hardware: Platforms named only as win2012 HDD, win10 SSD, mac SSD, linux SSD; CPU models not stated
tradeoffs: co/log is part of the coost base library (flags, coroutines, JSON, RPC, allocator in one package), so using it means pulling in coost's flag system and runtime; requires a C++17 compiler.
caveats: First-party README numbers only: no compiler, flags, library versions or CPU models, and the repo's benchmark directory (atomic, idgen, mem, rand, string, time, xtoa) has no log, glog or spdlog test, so the tables cannot be reproduced from the repo. The glog rows are write speeds on different storage (HDD/SSD) and OS combinations, and spdlog's configuration (sink, sync or async mode, version) is not stated. Coost also publishes co/json vs rapidjson (twitter.json minified, stringify/parse in microseconds: win 569/924 vs 2089/2495, mac 783/1097 vs 1289/1658, linux 468/764 vs 1359/1070, claimed 1.4-3.6x), same tier-C caveats and one row (linux parse) where the ratio is 1.4x.
